fields.title: Calculating from the User, Not the Industry
fields.keyTakeaway: Target reliability is derived from what a person does upon failure, how often they come, and where the perceptibility threshold is, rather than from an industry figure.
fields.sections/0/blocks/0/text: Where does "99.9%" come from — and why does it mean different things for two products with the same number?
fields.sections/1/blocks/0/text: A target taken by analogy is either excessive or insufficient, and both options are expensive. Excessive eats up quarters of work on something nobody will notice. Insufficient imperceptibly destroys trust: users don't complain, they leave.
fields.sections/2/blocks/0/text: The right target is derived from three questions about the user.
fields.sections/2/blocks/1/text: **What does the person do when it doesn't work?** Waits — reliability can be lower. Leaves for a competitor — higher. Loses money or data — maximum.
fields.sections/2/blocks/2/text: A product people return to lives with 99.5%. A product where failure means a failed purchase — does not.
fields.sections/2/blocks/3/text: **How often do they come?** A user visiting once a month has a 0.1% chance of hitting a glitch — meaning practically never. A user visiting ten times a day will encounter it once every three months.
fields.sections/2/blocks/4/text: Hence an important consequence: **the probability of encountering a glitch is calculated per user, not per system.** For an active user, 99.9% is not "almost always works", but "something didn't open once a quarter".
fields.sections/2/blocks/5/text: **Where is the [[perceptibility-threshold|perceptibility threshold]]?** Below it, a glitch is not perceived as a problem. A failure lasting 4 seconds and disappearing after a retry is not remembered. Forty seconds are remembered. Between them is a boundary worth knowing because it determines what is worth paying for.
fields.sections/2/blocks/6/text: Next — **[[criticality|different targets for different scenarios]]**, as in `SC2-N1-L1`. A single figure for the entire product always means overpaying for one thing and underpaying for another.
fields.sections/3/blocks/0/text: The breakdown by three questions yielded a distribution differing from initial intuitions.
fields.sections/3/blocks/1/text: *Checkout.* The person leaves: they need to buy products now, and a neighboring app has them. Maximum target — 99.9%.
fields.sections/3/blocks/2/text: *Catalog.* The person waits or refreshes. Perceptibility threshold is high: short glitches are not remembered. 99.5% is enough.
fields.sections/3/blocks/3/text: *Order history.* Visited rarely, waited calmly. 99% — and this turned out to be a discovery: previously it was protected on par with checkout.
fields.sections/3/blocks/4/text: *Partner dashboard.* The partner won't leave over half an hour, but will complain. 99.5%.
fields.sections/3/blocks/5/text: *Partner webhooks.* Losing an event is worse than a delay — here the target is not about availability, but delivery.
fields.sections/3/blocks/6/text: Recalculating probability per user changed the conversation about the catalog. At 99.5%, an active user visiting twice a day encounters a glitch about once every three months. Acceptable. For checkout, the same arithmetic at 99.5% would give one failed purchase per 200 — with an average check of 2,400 this is noticeable, and the figure was raised.
fields.sections/4/blocks/0/text: Measured reliability and perceived reliability diverge. Glitches for users with poor network, client app errors, slow internet — none of this makes it into SLIs, but all of it makes it into the impression.
fields.sections/5/blocks/0/text: Target reliability is derived from what a person does upon failure, how often they come, and where the perceptibility threshold is, rather than from an industry figure.
